A joint venture of Tŝideldel First Nation, Tl’etinqox Government, and Yunesit’in Government continues to be recognized for its contributions to Indigenous economic development through forest rehabilitation, wildfire risk reduction, and local employment across the Cariboo Chilcotin. Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation Ltd. (CCR) recently received the 2026 Cando (Council for the Advancement of Native Development Officers) Indigenous Private Sector Business Award. The award was presented during the non-profit society’s annual national conference held Oct. 5 to Oct. 8 in Victoria as part of its Economic Developer of the Year Awards. In a news release, CCR CEO and elected councillor of Tŝideldel First Nation Percy Guichon called it a proud moment for CCR and the communities behind it. “We have a lot of damaged forests in our territories, and we’ve worked hard to rehabilitate that land while creating jobs and opportunities for our people,” he stated. “This award recognizes the crews, communities, businesses, and partners who have helped us get this work done.” According to its webpage, CCR was originally formed as a joint venture between the Tŝideldel First Nation and Tl’etinqox Government in the spring of 2017 to address the 100,000 hectares of dead pine left in the Chilcotin region and to rehabilitate those stands into productive forests. In summer 2017, fires amplified the need to address heavily burned forest stands with minimal economic value. Yunesit’in Government joined the joint venture in 2024. Member nations are provided a direct role in forestry projects within their territories while building local skills and business opportunities which Philippe Theriault, General Manager of TŝiDelDel Enterprises, said makes a difference for their communities. Courtney Samways is the owner of Seamaiden Boutique located in downtown Williams Lake and now open seven days a week until Christmas. Among the volunteers with the Cariboo Memorial Hospital Auxiliary Society Gift Shop is Val Fleming and Linda Symynuk. ‘Tis the season for holiday shopping and in Williams Lake there are many local shops already in the Christmas spirit to help you find the best home decor and gifts for loved ones that you might even buy extra for yourself. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says he wants B.C. public service workers to return to the office — though he is open to some exceptions for rural workers. “I’m committed to having people come back to the office,” he said. Working from home has expanded drastically since the COVID-19 pandemic, including among B.C. government employees, many of whom work via “telework” agreements. Some employees are even hired with this in mind, with some teams consisting of workers scattered throughout the province. Doerkson says he is open to flexible work arrangements for people living in remote or rural parts of the province, but wants those living near population centres to come into work. “I’m open to the notion that we might have a hybrid where we have people working in very rural spaces or rural parts of our province,” he said at a news conference at a government office in Victoria. “But the reality is if you’re living in a place that’s accessible to an office, like this that’s in downtown Victoria or elsewhere in the province in some of our other centres, I want people coming back to work in the office.” A spokesperson for Doerkson clarified that no decisions have been made yet regarding how this will work, and a firm plan won’t be revealed until after he is sworn in on Nov. 20. Roughly 36,000 of these public service workers are members of the B.C. General Employees Union. About one-third are frontline workers who could not work remotely, such as BC Liquor store employees or corrections officers. Union president Paul Finch says he is “optimistic” to hear Doerkson say he is open to a hybrid arrangement for rural workers. But Finch says he has not yet spoken with Doerkson, and is reserving judgment until he gets more information. Crown counsellor Catherine Rezansoff argued the opposite, telling the court that even if the complainant’s testimony is not believed, the accused’s testimony itself proves he did not obtain consent. Crown added that the accused did not take reasonable steps to ensure consent. Rezansoff argued Hildebrand Acosta did not ensure the complainant was awake, suggesting the accused was actually attempting not to wake the complainant. Rezansoff told the court the complainant, in the accused’s own testimony, had turned her back to Hildebrand Acosta after he claims to have asked her to “hook up”, and did not touch or kiss the accused and did not assist in pulling her pants down. 77feeca07c1657fc47b65a09e8020dfd.text: 3 arrested in Fort St. James after threats of extortion, violence | Williams Lake Tribune 3 arrested in Fort St. James after threats of extortion, violence Fort St. James RCMP arrested three people on Nov. 11, 2026 in connection with threats of extortion and violence. Three people were ultimately arrested in connection with an extortion investigation that involved two of the suspects allegedly fleeing from police. Fort St. James RCMP say the three will remain in police custody until they can attend court, according to a news release Thursday (Nov. 12). Police first received information about threats of extortion and violence toward a resident on Wednesday. There was also a possibility of a firearm in the suspect’s possession, RCMP said. Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, the B.C. RCMP’s northern spokesperson, said that based on the information provided to police, the decision was made to bring in the North District Emergency Response Team. The team was assisted by the police dog unit and RCMP air services. Officers found the suspect in a vehicle near the intersection of Eagle Drive and Garvie Road, the release says. Two other people were also in the vehicle. However, police say that when officers tried a traffic stop, the driver fled from police. RCMP pursued and the vehicle was followed to the 2700-block of Lind Lake Pit Road, the release says. The driver stopped and two people got out of the vehicle and allegedly fled from police on foot. The third person stayed in the vehicle and was arrested. During a search of the vehicle, police found and seized two firearms. Police found the other two suspects a “short distance away” and both were arrested.

aaaf770217e8a85f4739cc230b32f528.text: Felix Townsin visits Parliament Hill to share his vision with MPs and senators. An Esquimalt teen is punching above his weight, taking his pitch to Parliament to create A Million Acts of Love Month in Canada. A Million Acts of Love revolves around the memory of Felix Townsin’s little sister Lexi, who lived with Blau syndrome and died of complications just shy of her seventh birthday in 2019. Felix was nine, but he’d already been involved in philanthropic efforts, writing Don’t Floss Your Toes at age 5 as a fundraiser for Blau syndrome (early-onset sarcoidosis) and juvenile arthritis. In 2024, Felix Townsin set out to inspire one million acts of love in Lexi’s memory, before what would have been her 12th birthday. In 2025, the Royal Bay Grade 11 student and his family officially formed A Million Acts of Love Foundation, a grassroots charity funding youth projects that build community. That year, Esquimalt proclaimed the month Nov. 16 to Dec. 16 – with the end date landing on Lexi’s birthday – A Million Acts of Love Month. This year, the 16-year-old is petitioning for Canada to recognize A Million Acts of Love Month from Nov. 16 to Dec. 16, ending on Lexi’s birthday. Felix was invited to Parliament Hill to share his vision with members of parliament and senators, an “incredible opportunity,” notes a Nov. 6 Me My Dad and Blau social media post. “He’s a busy Grade 11 student taking double the course load just to fit in leadership, social justice and band classes, while helping support nearly 100 incredible young Changemakers and their projects and still trying to create opportunities for even more youth,” the post reads. “And one of the hardest parts has been something we never expected… getting people to sign his petition to recognize A Million Acts of Love Month across Canada.” When the post went live, it had 393 of the required 500 signatures. f896d0f44a21babfa0104e0571dcde17.text: You may hear or see a CC-295 Kingfisher airplane southwest of Williams Lake dropping smoke or illumination flares as the Canadian Armed Forces train in the Chilcotin Range from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20. Airplanes may be seen dropping smoke or illumination flares west of Williams Lake in the coming days as the Canadian Armed Forces train in the sky. According to a public service announcement, aircraft from 19 Wing Comox will be training from Monday, Nov. 16 to Friday, Nov. 20 between 6 p.m. and 1 a.m. in the Chilcotin Military Training Area to maintain their night operation capabilities. “During this period, members of the public may hear or see one of the squadron’s CC-295 Kingfisher airplanes in the area dropping smoke or illumination flares,” the announcement stated. “These bright white flares can be seen from a great distance as they slowly descend from the sky to the water and burn for four to five minutes each.” The essential training will ensure the Royal Canadian Air Force’s (RCAF) Search and Rescue (SAR) crews are able to safely conduct night rescues. “RCAF SAR Technicians are known for their distinctive bright orange jumpsuits and commitment to helping Canadians in peril,” the announcement further added. “Regular training under a variety of conditions ensures that the SAR techs are always ready to meet whatever challenges, day or night, that a mission may present.”

29329d980313831e5ab4a0e75c0066c5.text: A “communication issue” has led to a ground stop for all U.S. airport by the Federal Aviation Administration. The grounding of flights at all U.S. airports is beginning to have international impacts. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop Friday afternoon (Nov. 13), citing telecommunications issues. The agency said in a post to X that a temporary telecommunications outage has led to the ground stop “out of an abundance of caution.” The post adds that every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis. The post did not say when the outage could be resolved or when the ground stop could be lifted. An update had not been provided by 5:36 p.m. Pacific Time. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy posted to social media at 2:16 p.m. Pacific Time that the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following the “communication issue” that is impacting all air route traffic control centres. He added that Federal Aviation Administration technicians are investigating the issue. U.S.-bound flights are showing as “delayed” on multiple major Canadian airport departure flight trackers. Vancouver International Airport says it’s seeing delays for U.S.-bound flights, as well as some international routes that would fly over U.S. airspace. Initially, the airport said domestic flights are not impacted. However, an update at 5:11 p.m. from YVR says “airlines are adjusting flight schedules accordingly, which is causing cancellations to U.S. destinations, and some delays and cancellations to international and domestic flights at YVR. Toronto Pearson International Airport says international and domestic flights are continuing to operate out of the airport “where routes do not require transit through U.S. airspace.”

c694d23a6de94123bbe1ec3cac6ad0c0.text: Members of the Okanagan Indian Band filled a small courtroom in Kelowna the morning of Nov. 13 to listen to the appeal for a man no longer allowed in their community. Donald Ashley, a First Nations healer, appeared at the Kelowna Law Courts to appeal his 2025 sentence for simple assault of a client in 2022. Ashley was originally charged with six counts of sexual assault for allegations of inappropriate touching of six complainants during one-on-one healing sessions in October 2022. One of the charges was stayed at the start of the trial, and two more charges were dropped according to the direction of the presiding judge. Ashley was found guilty by a jury in 2024 of one count of simple assault. Sentenced later that year, as reported by IndigiNews, Ashley did not receive any jail time, but a two-year probation order with a one-year ban on offering healing sessions and the second-year order requiring healing sessions to be conducted with supervision and client-signed waivers. Defence counsel for Ashley, Mark Iyengar and Mark Nohra, argued the sentence issued was an error in judgement by the sentencing judge and demonstrably unfit for the charge, requesting a discharge. Iyengar told the three-judge panel that his client’s sentence was issued in error and more weight should have been placed on the therapeutic context of the touching. Defence stated the inference should be made that the touching was for healing purposes and not for self-gratification. Defence also argued the community impact statement was incorrectly considered by the sentencing judge, as it had been edited before being submitted to the court and the overall sentiment had changed. Nohra followed his colleague by stating that Ashley’s sentence was demonstrably unfit, having caused him mental health struggles, financial hardships, and a disconnect from his Indigenous roots as he’s been banned from all Okanagan band territories. f723e84b420eaac93fda8c7743d77e80.text: Elenore Sturko, CentreBC party leader and candidate in Surrey South, interviewed by TV crew on B.C. election night Oct. 24, 2026. Former Surrey MLA Elenore Sturko has announced she’s leaving partisan politics and will no longer be leader of the CentreBC party. Sturko ran as CentreBC leader in the Surrey South riding in the Oct. 24 provincial election, a seat won by former White Rock mayor and Conservative candidate Megan Knight. “I’m leaving partisan politics. I’ve decided to leave partisan politics behind and and concentrate on the new chapter,” Sturko said Friday (Nov. 13). ‘It’s something that I’ve been thinking about even before the election … with not being able to continue on as an MLA, I think that likely, the best opportunities for me to continue to serve my community will be along the lines of non-partisan politics.” Whether that’s in communications work or in policy, Sturko said finding ways to serve “outside the realm of politics is something that I look forward to.” Sturko was elected to the Surrey South riding in a 2022 byelection when former MLA Stephanie Cadieux left electoral politics to become Canada’s first Chief Accessibility Officer. She crossed the floor from the BC United party (formerly BC Liberals) to join the B.C. Conservative Party, and won as Conservative MLA or Surrey-Cloverdale in 2024 before being kicked out of Conservative caucus last September. She then became an independent MLA prior to serving as CentreBC party leader in 2026. Sturko, whose three children are all now in high school said she is really looking forward to spending more time with her spouse and children, and “being able to help out more at home and to be more involved every day with my kids.” She is hopeful CentreBC will keep growing, as a centrist party and political option for those who prefer not to vote Conservative or NDP. “(CentreBC party members) are still eager to continue to grow and to build the party, and I encourage them to keep doing that. d87e0c7babbcf15c9616d76b23e54bdd.text: Nelson track runner Matti Erickson has signed a pro contract with Nike. Now that his college career is over, Matti Erickson’s race is only just starting. The Nelson, B.C., track star has signed a pro contract with Nike Swoosh TC, which is the sportswear giant’s distance running team. The deal will see Erickson compete for Nike through 2028. Erickson graduated from the University of Oregon this year and considered becoming a math teacher, but ultimately decided that, at 23 years old, he still has plenty of track ahead of him. “I thought I’m just too far along in this journey to give up now,” he said. “I have unfinished business, unaccomplished goals that I still feel like I have the ability to accomplish even if they feel far away. And so for those reasons, I just feel like I’ve got too much in me still. I’m so unproven that it was no-brainer really.” Erickson was a star for the Oregon Ducks, during which he was also the first Canadian athlete to sign a name, image and likeness deal with Nike. He won the 800-metres race at the 2025 NCAA indoor championships, and that year also won silver in the outdoor championships. Erickson also competed for Canada at the World Athletics Championships in 2025. But his last season was hampered by injuries, which forced Erickson to pull out of the world indoor championships in Poland in March, and for Team Canada at the summer’s Commonwealth Games in Scotland. Erickson said he is healthy again, and will have plenty of time to prepare for his next race. “I’ve got a big chunk of time to just really dial in on the training, get used to the new program and new dynamics with the training partners and really focus on being as healthy as possible and maintaining the level of health that I do have right now.” Qualifying for and excelling at the World Athletics Championships, which is next held September 2027 in Beijing, is among Erickson’s goals for the coming year. Erickson failed to make it to the semifinals at the 2025 worlds in Tokyo.

e133fa6eb10c0e0e8c6b82820e989916.text: The northwest corner of the Pear Lake wildfire, pictured on July 31. A preliminary report into the post-wildfire hazards associated with the fire has now been released, indicating likely moderate to high impacts on local properties, highways, and infrastructure. A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. The Clinton Creek watershed (6,663 hectares) saw 86 per cent of its area burned, with 76 per cent of that burned at moderate or high severity. Some 50 per cent of the Big Bar Creek watershed (45,156 hectares in total) was burned, and 41 per cent of the Maiden Creek watershed (5,955 hectares) was burned. The report states that potential elements at risk include residential structures on private properties; First Nations lands; the Highway 97 and Highway 99 corridors; secondary public roads, including the Clinton-Pavilion Road and the southern part of Jesmond Road; provincial parks at Marble Range, Big Bar Lake, Downing, and Chasm; the CN rail mainline; the BC Hydro transmission line and substation near Kelly Lake; and water resources and infrastructure in the Clinton Community Watershed.

Police in Vancouver, along with the help of international partners, cracked down on a Russia-based cybercrime network. The RCMP Federal Policing Pacific Region cybercrime investigation team in Vancouver is the lead Canadian police agency in the international joint forces operation targeting initial access malware. It was dubbed Operation Endgame, according to a news release from RCMP Friday (Nov. 13). The Vancouver team contributed coders, analysts and investigators. Police say the Russia-based “Gootloader” malware enables unauthorized access to computer systems around the world through compromised websites. It uses infected WordPress websites to spread malware “masquerading as legal documents.” The team in Vancouver and the RCMP’s cyber and technical investigation service developed a tool that removes Gootloader malware from infected machines. That tool was then shared with Operation Endgame partners to “disrupt the malware on a global scale.” The week of Nov. 9, the police team from Vancouver were at Europol headquarters in The Hague, Netherlands to participate in global action week when the “disinfection tool” was deployed by law enforcement in Canada, Denmark, The Netherlands and the U.S. Police said during that time, approximately 672 infected websites were remediated globally. In Canada, the Vancouver team disinfected 24 compromised machines. RCMP added that Operation Endgame is the largest ongoing joint forces operation that has brought together law enforcement agencies from countries including Canada, Bulgaria, Denmark, Germany, Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom and the U.S. It’s supported by Europol and Eurojust. The Vancouver team has previously helped with Operation Endgame earlier this year, working to crack down on SocGholish, which is linked to the Russian cybercriminal group Evil Corp. A 108 Mile Ranch Volunteer Fire Department tender arrives on the scene of a fire at the South Cariboo Landfill. UPDATE: 100 Mile Fire Rescue extinguished an early morning fire at the South Cariboo Landfill on Friday, Nov. 13. 100 Mile Fire Rescue chief Dave Bissat said his department responded to the incident at 8:23 a.m. Friday morning. On arrival, he said crews discovered a fire in the Demolition, Land Clearing and Construction waste area that covered 100 feet by 100 feet. “Firefighters quickly brought the fire under control and continued working to extinguish remaining hot spots and complete overhaul operations to ensure the fire was fully extinguished,” Bissat said. “We also received assistance from 108 Mile Volunteer Fire Department and Lone Butte Volunteer Fire Department, who provided additional water supply support throughout the incident.” Bissat said crews had the fire fully extinguished and completed their operations by 1 p.m. He added that the exact cause of the fire remains undetermined at this time. “I would also like to thank the responding firefighters and our neighbouring departments for their assistance and teamwork in bringing this incident to a safe conclusion,” Bissat said. ORIGINAL STORY: A small wildfire has closed the South Cariboo Landfill on Friday, Nov. 13. Early in the morning on Friday, a small fire was discovered burning near the Cariboo Regional District’s South Cariboo Landfill. 100 Mile Fire Rescue responded and requested the assistance of the 108 Mile Volunteer Fire Department and Lone Butte Volunteer Fire Department. 97a3f4b485e2fa88ee630258d8074abf.text: Victoria's Inner Harbour and historic architecture helped earn the city a spot on the list. Victoria has been recognized as one of North America’s top 10 fairytale cities, thanks to its British-inspired architecture, historic landmarks and waterfront scenery. Travel Off Path released its list of 10 Fairytale Cities in North America on Oct. 31, placing Victoria seventh among destinations in Canada, the United States and Mexico. The list highlights cities offering European-style experiences without the need for a transatlantic flight. Victoria was compared to London and described as a destination known for its British colonial charm, manicured gardens and harbour walks. “Located on the southern tip of Vancouver Island, this city holds onto its British roots hard,” wrote Travel Off Path editor Tyler Fox. The B.C. Parliament Buildings overlooking the Inner Harbour were also highlighted for giving the city a regal, old-world atmosphere. Fox suggested visitors explore Victoria’s waterfront dining options rather than spend money on some of the city’s more expensive tourist experiences. Instead, he recommended visiting a local waterfront pub for fish and chips and a locally brewed beer. Victoria was one of three Canadian destinations included in the ranking. Quebec City claimed the top spot, with its historic stone buildings, French-speaking culture and fortified city walls earning comparisons to a traditional French village. Lunenburg, N.S., placed ninth, recognized for its colourful waterfront buildings, maritime heritage and historic architecture. Guanajuato, Mexico, ranked second for its colourful hillside homes and winding streets, while San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, took third place for its Spanish colonial architecture. Other destinations included Leavenworth, Wash., in fourth; Solvang, Calif., in fifth; Carmel-by-the-Sea, Calif., in sixth; St. Augustine, Fla., in eighth; and Ouray, Colo., in 10th. 3ca52d080a8bd836a67977ae457ade64.text: A West Kelowna woman was fined $368 when she was spotted driving with an open laptop on her lap during a traffic stop in Vernon on Nov. 5. Many people are still working remotely, but BC Highway Patrol (BCHP) is reminding drivers that vehicles are not offices, and using your laptop while operating a vehicle could land you with a steep fine. A 52-year-old West Kelowna woman found that out the hard way, and is now facing a $368 fine for allegedly driving while using her laptop during a recent BCHP distracted driving operation in Vernon. The stop occurred on Nov. 5, just after 4:30 p.m., when a BC Highway Patrol officer observed a blue Honda Pilot whose driver had an open laptop on her lap on Highway 97 (32 Street) in Vernon. “Driving is a complex task that requires your complete attention to deal with the unexpected,” says Sgt. Michael McLaughlin with BC Highway Patrol. “Just because you’re comfortable behind the wheel, and you have something you ‘need’ to do, doesn’t mean the rules of the road don’t apply to you.” The driver of the blue Honda was issued a ticket for use of an electronic device while driving, which comes with a fine of $368. The ticket also includes four penalty points on their driver’s licence. Drivers who have two or more distracted driving tickets in a three-year period will also pay a Driver Risk Premium. This could see the total financial penalty rise to as much as $2,000, in addition to the regular insurance premium.
